summary: Defines an anonymous login mechanism for the SASL framework. Since plain text logins are not allowed in new IETF protocols, a standard way is needed to log in as an anonymous guest. It was replaced by RFC 4505.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2245 defines the ANONYMOUS mechanism for SASL. A client can request guest access and optionally provide trace information; the server decides whether to allow access and usually restricts it. RFC 4505 later obsoleted this memo.

questions: how to log in anonymously with sasl
what does the sasl anonymous mechanism send
can anonymous sasl prove who a user is
what security limits apply to anonymous sasl access
subtitle: A SASL mechanism for requesting anonymous access to a service.

tldr.problem: Services need a standard way to offer anonymous access within SASL without relying on plaintext login commands.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends one ANONYMOUS message containing an email address, an opaque trace token, or no trace information.

sections.title: Anonymous Access with SASL
sections.content: Internet services commonly allow anonymous access. Traditionally, a user could log in as anonymous and provide optional trace information as a plaintext password. The RFC says plaintext login commands are not permitted in new IETF protocols, so it defines a way to request anonymous access within SASL.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask a service for guest access without sending a password. The ANONYMOUS mechanism provides a standard SASL request for that access.

sections.title: The ANONYMOUS Client Message
sections.content:
The mechanism name is ANONYMOUS. It consists of one client message containing optional human-readable trace information: an Internet email address, an opaque token without an @ character, or nothing. The RFC recommends using an email address only with the user's permission. An opaque token can be up to 255 printable US-ASCII characters excluding @.

A server that permits anonymous access announces support for ANONYMOUS and allows anyone to log in with it, usually with restricted access.
sections.plainLanguage: The client may send an email address, an opaque token, or no trace information. This identifies the request as anonymous; it does not prove who sent it.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Limits
sections.content:
The RFC advises administrators to disable anonymous access by default and restrict its capabilities. Anonymous write access can fill storage; shared read and write access can enable anonymous exchanges; and expensive operations or connections without idle timeouts can enable denial of service. A drop-box model can accept submissions without allowing anonymous users to read them.

Trace information is not authenticated and can be falsified. Clients should not send a user's email address without permission. Anonymous connections can also be subject to man-in-the-middle attacks, so the RFC encourages external integrity and encryption mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Guest access should be limited because it can consume resources or expose data. Trace details can be false, and the connection itself is not protected by this mechanism.
